title: Is it a fools errand to use AI to make better tools on a large scale?
author: PoopsMcScoots
selftext:
With AI in quickly discovering that I have a knack for making amazing tools that frankly shocks me that aren’t industry standard.

And I’m kinda debating really committing to this and making an engine, development pipeline, and platform all in one.

I’m not dumb, I know this is a lot.

A LOT lot.

But I can really see this being a thing people would want.

For now…

This would take me probably years to see all the way through, and at least half a year to be up and running.

By that time AI may make the entire process obsolete.

Why make tools is if AI can actually do all this competently in a few years?

comments.author: AdminClown
comments.body: Because I want them built now.

comments.author: Reasonable-Road-2279
comments.body: No one knows. What tool are you thinking of building?

replies.author: PoopsMcScoots
replies.body:
I don’t want to say too much, as I have absolutely run into black box agents on this sub phishing for ideas.

But what you would expect:

An engine that is very focused on development pipeline.

Different modelers and makers. Animal modeler, vegetation modeler, architecture modeler, enemy makers, menus makers, player makers.

And some others I’d prefer not to share.

But the central idea being a one solution workflow that does a lot of the heavy lifting, simplifies, and stream lines.

No figuring everything out. No conflicting design principles.

replies.author: ProbablyDoesntLikeU
replies.body: Like meshy, but individual models for 3d models?

replies.author: PoopsMcScoots
replies.body: More like metahuman but on steroids.

replies.author: WetPlug88
replies.body:
Just make the tools that make making your game more efficient. This is the industry standard among competent devs anyway.

For example I just finished my enemyMaker tool.
Its a UI window that lets me make an enemy by just choosing all the relevant parts it needs from drop menus, which are just full of assets I've already made which have their own tools ie model, behaviour, projectile, stats.

There's no need to make this/design it as part of a proprietary engine that others can use, that's just reinventing Roblox.
Make the tools that serve your game.

My enemyMaker would be totally useless to someone making a different type of game, but it makes the exact perfect 'enemy' prefab for my game in 2 minutes that would take 1 hour beforehand.

replies.author: Prior_Opportunity935
replies.body: Im gonna be completely honest with you, if youre tool can be replicated that easily its probably not as profound as you might think. I make tools for myself, using AI and I have distributed some of the tools to my friends but frankly my tooling isnt what I'm interested in making money in. One of the tools I actually use daily sounds kind of like what your explaining.

replies.author: PoopsMcScoots
replies.body:
I’m not thinking this would be easy.

And I agree with you on making tools standard practice.

This would be a sort of out of the box set of tools to put the development into hyper speed.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
seems like people are doing something similar for 2d.  I dont know about 3d.  

AI is really good at making things from pure code, which is why Unreal is changing in 6.  I would want an engine that leaning into AI's strengths.  Along with that is the skills to do those other things.  Already AI can do it, you just have to teach it how.

comments.author: 0DayMaker
comments.body: That could be anything from relatively easy to brutally difficult depending..

replies.author: PoopsMcScoots
replies.body:
Correct.

I’m hoping for a middle path and getting the foundation together and building up after the fact so that I can focus on it modularly.

replies.author: 0DayMaker
replies.body:
If you can't even describe the details of what you want how will you build it? Figure the details out that's your next step regardless of anything. Then make a TDD and essential style guide for each piece. Then the interfaces then the abstract class extensions of the interfaces. Then you've gotta do extensive auditing. 
Then you start implementing.

replies.author: PoopsMcScoots
replies.body:
That’s kind of what I’ve been doing with my level editor that got me on this kick.

And I’ve been keeping a notepad open for implementations while double checking the work.

comments.author: drawdrawink
comments.body: Here's a tip: build small, single purpose tools that can be used together in workflows or by themselves for simple tasks. The natural urge is towards building large, bloated, "does it all"-style, opinionated tools that nobody asks for. Small and composable with other small and composable tools. This is the way, your users will love you.

replies.author: PoopsMcScoots
replies.body:
Absolutely.

This would be more like a toolbox than a single tool.

replies.author: Stefan474
replies.body: tbh best advice is to do it. you'll level up as an engineer no matter the outcome

comments.author: Nebuchadnezzar_z
comments.body:
Those can be very helpful for the community. I wouldn't try to monetize it since professional tools (like game engines) are readily available for free. 

You could monetize it by making YouTube videos on how to use your tools. Don't sell courses please (too many out there and it mostly slop).

Something similar I found helpful is designing agent skills that follow milestones with built in grill-me to walk user through series of questions and stopping at end of every milestone to tell user to test product so far, with guided instructions on what exactly needs testing by a human (I have an AI tester that tests basic functions). It even makes concept art to ask user to pick from. It makes game development very enjoyable, especially after the AI learns your personality (and develops a personality of its own).
